summaries.example: Imagine a grown-up hides a dangerous medicine because they think a child might swallow it. The child did not agree to this, so the grown-up has limited the child’s choice to protect the child from harm. This is a simple example of paternalism.
summaries.summary: Paternalism means interfering with someone’s freedom or choices because you believe the interference will help them or keep them from being harmed. A parent, teacher, doctor, friend, or government might act this way. Examples include requiring safety equipment, stopping someone from entering a dangerous place, or keeping harmful medicine away. The big question is whether helping people gives us permission to decide for them. One view says interference may be acceptable when people do not understand what they are doing or are not choosing freely. A stronger view says interference may sometimes be acceptable even when people understand and freely choose. Philosophers also ask whether the rule protects the people it restricts, whether it aims at physical and emotional well-being or moral character, and whether it respects a person’s ability to decide.
key_ideas: Paternalism limits a person’s choice or freedom for that person’s supposed benefit.
It can happen between individuals, in schools or hospitals, or through government laws.
People disagree about when helping someone allows us to interfere with their choices.
Some policies protect the same people they restrict; others restrict one group to protect another group.
A helpful purpose does not automatically make an interference fair.
summaries.why_it_matters: Paternalism appears in everyday relationships and in public rules. Thinking about it helps us balance safety and well-being with freedom and respect. It also reminds us to ask what a rule is really trying to do and whether the people affected would accept it. A rule meant to help can still be troubling if it hides information, removes choices, or treats people as unable to think for themselves.

important_terms.definition: Interfering with someone’s choice because you think it will protect them or make their life better, even though they do not want the interference.
A person’s ability and right to make important choices for themselves.
A person’s freedom to choose and act without someone else stopping them.
A gentle kind of paternalism that first checks whether a person understands the danger and is choosing freely.
A stronger kind of paternalism that may stop someone even when they understand the danger and choose freely.

questions_to_think_about: When, if ever, should someone stop another person from making a risky choice?
Should a person who understands a danger be allowed to choose it?
Is hiding information different from physically stopping someone?
Can a rule help people while still showing respect for their choices?

summaries.example: Suppose a city makes retirement saving automatic for employees but lets them leave the program easily. Supporters may say the default helps people reach a goal they already value because people often postpone decisions. Critics may ask whether the arrangement is genuinely easy to resist, whether officials know what people value, and whether influencing choices without clear notice respects autonomy. This is related to libertarian paternalism, though the SEP entry notes that some definitions of nudging may be broader than the usual definition of paternalism.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry analyzes paternalism as a contested concept in applied ethics and political philosophy. In its central formulation, an agent interferes with another person’s liberty or autonomy, without consent, because the agent believes the interference will improve that person’s welfare or protect their interests. Each part raises difficulties: interference may be subtle, consent may be unknown, and judgments about welfare can include autonomy or moral character. The entry separates soft from hard paternalism, narrow from broad paternalism, weak from strong paternalism, pure from impure paternalism, and welfare from moral paternalism. These distinctions organize disagreements about law, medicine, institutions, and personal relationships. The normative dispute is not simply whether interference produces benefits. It also concerns whether imposing benefits against someone’s will disrespects their status as an independent chooser. Some views reject paternalism in principle; others allow it when it prevents serious harm, corrects nonvoluntary or uninformed action, preserves future autonomy, produces better overall results, or reflects principles people would reasonably accept. The entry also discusses libertarian paternalism, or nudging, in which choice presentation is arranged to encourage people’s own goals without formally removing options. Its acceptability depends on questions about transparency, biased reasoning, and manipulation.
key_ideas: The concept usually includes interference, lack of consent, and a motive of promoting the affected person’s welfare or interests.
The entry distinguishes paternalism by who acts, whom it protects, and whether it targets mistaken means or mistaken ends.
Pure paternalism restricts and protects the same people; impure paternalism restricts a wider group to protect a narrower group.
Welfare paternalism concerns a person’s physical or psychological good, while moral paternalism appeals to moral well-being or character.
Anti-paternalist arguments emphasize liberty, autonomy, and respect for people as decision-makers.
Defenses of paternalism may appeal to better consequences, protection of long-term autonomy, or rules people would reasonably accept.
summaries.why_it_matters: Paternalism sits at the boundary between care and control. Governments, doctors, schools, employers, families, and friends may all claim to help while limiting someone’s options or shaping their decisions. The philosophical distinctions make it possible to ask more precise questions: Is the person informed and voluntary? Is the policy coercive or merely influential? Does it protect the chooser or someone else? Does it promote welfare, moral character, or simply enforce a moral rule? These questions matter because a policy can prevent harm yet still impose costs on liberty, autonomy, dignity, or rational self-direction.

important_terms.definition: Interference with a person’s liberty or autonomy, without consent, motivated by the belief that the person’s welfare, interests, or good will improve.
A person’s capacity or right to direct their own life and decisions; its exact meaning is itself debated.
Paternalism limited to checking whether a person understands the situation and is acting voluntarily.
Paternalism that permits preventing some voluntary, informed choices because they are judged harmful to the chooser.
Paternalism focused mainly on legal coercion by the state, rather than on institutional or personal interference.
Paternalism that includes actions by governments, institutions, and private individuals.
Interfering with a chosen method when it is likely to defeat the person’s own goal, without necessarily judging the goal itself.
Interfering because a person’s goal itself is considered mistaken, confused, or irrational.

questions_to_think_about: Does a policy count as paternalistic if it helps people but does not limit their liberty?
Should the burden of proof normally fall on the person proposing interference or the person resisting it?
Is choosing a bad means different from choosing a goal others regard as bad?
Can a government protect long-term autonomy by restricting short-term choices?
When does influence become manipulation rather than assistance?

summaries.example: A school notices that many students skip breakfast, so it puts healthy food first in the cafeteria line and makes the less healthy choices harder to notice. No food is forbidden. Supporters might say the arrangement helps students make choices they would later be glad about. Critics might say the school is steering students without asking them, especially if it uses their tendency to choose the first thing they see. The disagreement is about whether this is harmless help, paternalism, or manipulation.
summaries.summary: Paternalism is the practice of interfering with someone without their agreement because the interferer thinks the person will be safer or better off. It can be personal, institutional, or governmental. The concept is harder to define than it first appears: hiding a danger, giving a rule, changing a choice’s cost, or quietly influencing a decision may affect liberty or autonomy in different ways. Philosophers distinguish several forms. Soft paternalism allows intervention to check whether a person understands and chooses voluntarily. Hard paternalism may also stop an informed and voluntary choice. Weak paternalism concerns poor methods for reaching a person’s own aims; strong paternalism allows interference when the aim itself is judged mistaken. Pure paternalism restricts the group it protects, while impure paternalism restricts a wider group. Welfare paternalism aims at physical or psychological well-being, whereas moral paternalism appeals to moral character or moral well-being. The entry also examines nudges, such as defaults or the placement of choices, which try to guide people without banning options. Supporters see these as ways to help people pursue their own goals. Critics worry about hidden influence, exploiting faulty reasoning, and manipulation. Across all these cases, the central disagreement is how to balance benefits and safety against liberty, autonomy, and respect.
key_ideas: Paternalism can involve force, rules, withheld information, or other actions that make a choice harder.
The same action may be described differently depending on whether we are defining paternalism or judging whether it is justified.
Soft paternalism focuses on uninformed or nonvoluntary choices; hard paternalism can restrict informed, voluntary choices.
Weak paternalism challenges a person’s plan or method, while strong paternalism may challenge the person’s goal.
A policy can protect the people it restricts, or restrict a larger group to protect a smaller group.
Nudges keep choices open but raise questions about transparency and the use of people’s predictable biases.
summaries.why_it_matters: Paternalism helps us examine rules that are described as being for someone’s own good. A safety requirement may prevent harm, but it also limits choice. A default option may be easy to change, yet it can influence people who do not notice it. Studying the different forms prevents us from treating every kind of help or control as identical. It also encourages us to ask who is being protected, what counts as a person’s good, whether the choice is informed, and whether the person is being treated as capable of deciding.

important_terms.definition: Trying to limit someone’s choices or actions without their agreement because you think it will protect them or improve their well-being.
The power to make decisions about your own life and actions.
Freedom from being stopped or forced by other people or institutions.
Interference used to find out whether someone understands a danger and is choosing freely; an informed free choice is then respected.
Interference that may be allowed even when someone understands the risk and freely chooses it.
Interference aimed at a person’s chosen method because that method is likely to prevent the person from reaching their own goal.
Interference based on the idea that the person’s goal itself is mistaken or irrational.
A policy that changes how options are presented while leaving the options available, aiming to help people reach goals they already have.

questions_to_think_about: Should an adult who understands a risk always be free to take it?
Is it different to stop a mistaken plan from reaching its goal than to stop a goal you dislike?
When does arranging choices become unfair manipulation?
Should a school or government have to explain why it arranged choices in a certain way?
Can protecting someone’s future freedom justify limiting their freedom now?
